newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says missile deal with France aborted.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says missile deal with France aborted.

text.p: Taipei said on Monday its deal to buy shoulder-fired Mistral missiles from France had collapsed but would not comment on reports that pressure from arch rival China was to blame.
Taiwan nonetheless has succeeded in buying U.S.-made Stinger shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles, getting a low price because some were inventoried items, defence officials said.

"Because the Mistral budget has been listed for two years, and because France was unable to confirm the time to sign the deal with us...we decided to buy the U.S. Stingers first," Defence Minister Chiang Chung-ling told parliament.

Chiang rebuffed a call by deputies to say whether the aborted deal reflected pressure from Beijing, which regards Taiwan as a rebel province that must be brought under mainland sovereignty and should not be armed by China's diplomatic partners.
Under intense pressure from Beijing, Paris agreed in 1994 to halt all new arms sales to Taiwan. But it intends to complete transfer of 60 Mirage 2000-5 fighter jets purchased in 1992.
Chiang declined to say if Taiwan's military would continue to seek Mistral sales from France and how much Taiwan had offered for the weapons.
Taipei's Liberty Times said the 2,000 Mistrals and shoulder launchers were worth T$10 billion (US$360 million).
Chiang said Taiwan did succeed in buying a number of Stinger missiles from the United States, but declined to give details of their price or quantity.
He denied a Liberty Times report on Monday that the Stingers were old and "soon-to-be decommissioned".
Lawmaker Yen Chin-fu of the pro-independence opposition Democratic Progressive Party chided Chiang for buying "old stuff" from the U.S.
"If you say it is not 'sucker diplomacy,' then what is it?" he told Chiang in parliament.

Army chief of staff Huo Shou-yeh said Taiwan received a 40 percent discount on one-sixth of the Stingers because they were inventoried items and six to seven years old, putting the price at US$56,000 each instead of US$100,000 for new ones.
"The inventory items still can be used for 10 to 16 years and we can use them for practice purposes," Huo said, noting that the rest of the missiles were new.
The United States is Taiwan's major arms supplier despite a lack of formal diplomatic relations.
Washington, which since 1979 has recognised Beijing as the sole government of China, is under pressure from China to stop arming the Nationalist-ruled island.
